# Tesakuṇajātaka (Ja 521)

**ID:** Ja 521
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Three Birds

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tesakuṇajātaka* (Ja 521), titled *Three Birds* in English, is a birth story set at Jetavana, where the Buddha admonishes the King of Kosala on righteous statecraft (*dhammena rajjaṁ kāretabbaṁ*) [SuttaCentral; Emmanuel 2013; Fausböll 1891]. The Master warns the king that royal misconduct corrupts officials and leads to suffering, contrasting the misery of sensual indulgence with the blessings of abstaining from evil courses [SuttaCentral; Emmanuel 2013]. To illustrate royal virtue, the Buddha narrates a past life in which King Brahmadatta of Benares, being without a son, adopted three eggs from a nest in his royal park—an owl, a myna bird (*sālikā*), and a parrot—rearing them as royal foster children under the names Vessantara, Kuṇḍalinī, and Jambuka [Winternitz 1933; Migot 1954]. When grown, the three exceptionally wise birds instruct the king in *rājadharma* (the duties and ethical conduct of a ruler) [Winternitz 1933]. At the story's conclusion, the Bodhisatta is identified as the parrot Jambuka, with the other birds identified with Sāriputta, Uppalavaṇṇā, and Ānanda [Fausböll 1891; Migot 1954].

The text serves as an important source for early Buddhist political philosophy [Emmanuel 2013; Tambiah 1976]. The birds counsel the monarch to eliminate wrath, arrogance, and falsehood, to judge equitably, govern justly, protect subjects from violence, and restrain the senses [Moore 2016; Emmanuel 2013]. It asserts that divine fortune (Lakṣmī) favors bold, benevolent, and virtuous sovereigns rather than capricious or oppressive rulers [Shaw 2006]. The discourse also articulates the doctrine of the five royal strengths (*balāni*) underpinning legitimate kingship: physical strength of arms (*bāhabalaṁ*), material wealth (*bhogabalaṁ*), counsel of ministers (*amaccabalaṁ*), high birth (*abhijaccabalaṁ*), and intellectual wisdom (*paññābalaṁ*), which is esteemed as the greatest among them [Tambiah 1976].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include a full narrative counterpart in the Buddhist Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (Mvu 27) [SuttaCentral; Jones 1949], an affinity confirmed by DharmaNexus, which computes automated alignments between Ja 521 and the *Mahāvastu* with matching scores reaching 90 [DharmaNexus; Moore 2016; Winternitz 1933]. DharmaNexus additionally identifies text reuse with Tibetan canonical texts, including the *Rājāvavādaka-mahāyāna-sūtra* and the *Udānavarga* [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, SuttaCentral notes a reference to the work in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.11) [SuttaCentral], while DharmaNexus records significant verse reuse across multiple volumes of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as shared passages with the *Ummādantījātaka* (Ja 527), *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka* (Ja 540), and the *Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho* [DharmaNexus].
